utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Could we have the appearances for the day, starting with the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, counsel, good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. Mark Harmon, April Carter, Bronagh McKenna, Barney Thomas, Rafael La Cruz, and Carmela Javier for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Harmon. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dee Montgomery, Tina Drolec, Chad Mair, Boris Zorko, Gregor Guy-Smith and Novak Lukic appearing on behalf of Mr. Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, before I start my remarks of today, I was looking over the transcript last night and noted two areas where I'd like to make a correction and an addition. The correction is at page 14769 at line 24, it indicates footnote 619, should be footnote 1619. Also, when I was discussing the issue of the Lilic/Perisic intercept in regards to figuring out a way of influencing Mr. Mladic, I mentioned at page 14791, lines 12 through 20, P886 and I would like it to add to that, P1464.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'd like to turn my attention now to the discussion that has been had with regard to the issue of Zuc. It is absolutely clear from the discussions that have been had concerning much of the evidence, but clearly when it comes to the issue of Zuc, that although there's an agreement on many of the facts, the perception of how one is to interpret those facts is quite distinct. The Prosecution presented evidence of a military operation. The Chamber received evidence that that military operation was a failure, that men from the 72nd died, that territory was lost, and that the purpose of that particular operation, that being capturing, holding, and controlling Zuc did not occur. Now, whether there would have been a different result and whether that would have had a substantial effect on the commission of crimes is no longer an issue which is on the table because there was not a different result, it was a limited incident and there is no evidence that was offered to the Chamber that establishes a nexus between the failed operation in Zuc and the bombing or shelling of Sarajevo. The fact that both of these incidents occurs in and of itself does not establish a nexus. It would be convenient if it did, but it doesn't, and by indicating that two separate factual matters occurred, does not establish proof that there is a relationship between them or in this particular situation that there was a substantial effect, which is the test. Furthermore, I think it's very important that the Chamber go back and carefully review the cross-examination of MP-11 with regard to his claimed status, and I will leave it at that in terms of any further discussion in open session, and I will not go into private session. However, his assertion that he was present at a meeting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Don't you think you should go into private session, sir. I think you should.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, you also have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Hold on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You also have received other testimony with regard to the issue of Perisic's presence and that was from Zlatko Danilovic and Zlatko Danilovic was specifically asked whether he ever saw General Perisic, he answered he did not. And he was asked whether or not he ever heard about General Perisic being present, and once again his answer was that he had not. The conclusion drawn by Ms. Carter in her argument yesterday that they have established a nexus is inaccurate and wanting. Prosecution's failed to prove and the Defence contention that there's no nexus as between Zuc and the crimes charged remains. There's one other thing which is of some moment with regard to the argument that was made by Ms. Carter and that was the use of the term "trained snipers". I don't think that there would be any dispute that snipers are in fact used in war. They are a legitimate manner of fighting, and the fact that there were trained snipers at the failed operation does not forward the Prosecution's case whatsoever. It is, of course, something that would, I suggest, potentially cause some thought since there is an issue and there's been a discussion in which the word "sniper" has been used as it relates to Sarajevo, but the fact that once again there are trained snipers in a failed military operation does not necessarily, in any fashion whatsoever, establish that there was a substantial effect on whatever crimes were committed in Sarajevo. In the absence of there being a nexus, there has been a failure of proof. Mr. Harmon in his opening remarks mentioned, as did I, that a fair amount of his case is based on circumstantial evidence and I wish to just spend a moment reading a definition of that because I think it's of critical importance to this Chamber's consideration. "Circumstantial evidence may be of no less substance than direct evidence. However, a Trial Chamber must be cautious not to draw inferences based upon the assumptions rather than proven facts. As pointed out by the Trial Chamber in Krnojelac, 'While a number of different circumstances, which taken in combination, point to the existence of a particular fact upon which the guilt of the accused depends because they would usually exist in combination only because a particular fact did exist. Such a conclusion must be the only reasonable conclusion available.'" I repeat the last phrase: "The only reasonable conclusion available." If there is another conclusion available, Mr. Perisic is entitled to the benefit of that conclusion. Finally, once again in terms of the issue of perception, I want to discuss very briefly the issue of the French pilots and the measure of the man and what Perisic did. Now, we all recall that at the time that individuals went to get the French pilots, there was the Paris Peace Conference days away. We have received direct evidence from the highest of sources that the following was on the table: "We were rapidly approaching the formal peace conference in Paris. However, President Chirac had declared that it could not take place until two French pilots captured by the Bosnian Serbs when their aircraft was shot down over Pale on August 30th had been released. There was no reason to doubt his determination to make the meeting in Paris conditional on the release of the pilots." I'm a simple lawyer. I work in courtrooms --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before you go to the simple lawyer, as you quote, can you give us the speaker and the reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Absolutely. The speaker is Carl Bildt. The reference is page 14314, lines 5 through 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Surely. I still remain a simple lawyer and I don't understand how nations negotiate. I don't understand what is put on the table, but one thing is very clear, if the pilots had not been released, there would have been no Paris conference. Based on the information that has been presented to this Court, if there had been no Paris conference, there would have been no Dayton Peace Accord. Not only was a nation waiting for the return of these two gentlemen, the world was waiting for the return of these two gentlemen. And the issue of peace and cessation of hostilities was conditioned upon this release, and the evidence that you have received is that General Perisic was instrumental in obtaining the conditions that allowed for that release and allowed for the peace process to move forward. I turn the balance of our remarks at this time over to Mr. Lukic. In the event that I have failed to say anything with regard to those issues that I have addressed or that were the subject matter of my discussion, I'm not concerned. I do apologise, but I'm not concerned. And the reason for that is under this system where the Prosecution has the proof and bears that burden of the proof beyond a reasonable doubt, you, the Chamber, the fact-finders, are the find hurdle that the Prosecution must satisfy, and you, the Chamber, hold that particular obligation and that particular task and I'm confident that you will exercise that duty fully, responsibly and with great analysis and care. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to our colleagues from the Prosecution. Good morning to all the participants in these proceedings, especially to the interpreters who are now going to give their contribution to these proceedings of ours. I'm going to be speaking in my mother tongue. Your Honours, the first part of my remarks will be channelled towards challenging the charges that through his actions General Perisic provided the officer corps to the VRS and the SVK and in this way substantially contributed to the crimes that occurred in Sarajevo and Srebrenica. Finally, I'm going to speak about command responsibility, and ultimately, I will be speaking about the personality of Mr. Perisic and some of his personal actions. According to the indictment General Perisic continued with the practice of financing and providing most of the personnel who comprised the officer cadre of the VRS. The Defence never denied that part of the officers personnel, I repeat, part of the officers personnel of the VRS and SVK and for whom the Prosecution claims was -- were members of the Army of Yugoslavia were financed by the Army of Yugoslavia. However, the Prosecution thesis is based on the contribution given to that by the personnel centres and previously it is explained on the basis of ad hoc departures based on a voluntary joining of the troops there. The Prosecution is avoiding the wider evidence, as it were, what happened previously, how this functioned, and what happened after General Perisic was appointed Chief of General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia in August 1993. We do not wish to ignore that. When trying the facts, the Trial Chamber has to judge the actions of the accused, determining his personal participation, contribution to the commission of crimes, and that has to be significant. In our view, Your Honours, that means that you have to establish what General Perisic's significant contribution was to providing those officers in relation to the situation that prevailed before he became Chief of General Staff, especially the extent to which personnel centres affected this personnel and their stability. Let us be quite specific on this. The Defence claims that the Prosecution has not proven beyond reasonable doubt that since Perisic was appointed Chief of General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, there were significant changes as a result of his actions in providing officers for the Army of Republika Srpska and especially with respect to the stability and efficacy of these officers that the Prosecution refers to. The first question that I would like us to deal with in relation to these divergent positions between the parties is: Who comprised the personnel of the Army of Republika Srpska from the moment when that army was established? The next question is: What, and to what extent, General Perisic changed, which would constitute the actus reus of his incriminations among the personnel of Republika Srpska? It is important for you to establish in this respect, Your Honours, whether the Prosecutor proved their contention that the personnel centres maintained the vitality of that army, and that they made the command structure of that army sustainable, in Mr. Harmon's words. Who were the officers that comprised the command structure of the Army of Republika Srpska? According to the Prosecution, they were officers of the Army of Yugoslavia. The Defence asserts that the majority of these officers had the status of, initially, officers of the Army of Republika Srpska and that that was their status throughout the war. When the Law on the Army of Republika Srpska was passed in June, 1992 - P191, that is the relevant exhibit - of their own free will they became active-duty personnel of the Army of Republika Srpska in accordance with Article 377 of that law. There is a great deal of testimony and references to that effect in our final brief and I'm not going to quote any of that specifically now. From that moment onwards they became part of that single chain of command. They had their actual place within the establishment, and in any army, there can be only one for any particular officer. They held their respective ranks, their respective positions, they had their uniforms, they had their insignia, their emblems stating that they belonged to the Army of Republika Srpska. They had their own oath and they had their own subordinates.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Superiors.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They had orders, naredjenje and naredbe that they obeyed. According to the Law on the Army of Republika Srpska, they saw what the consequences would be if they did not obey these orders. What the specific responsibility involved was if they did not obey these orders. In a word, they were part of a functioning army within their chain of command established by law. Your Honours, there was nothing untruthful or concealed within that chain of command, nothing was fictitious either, nothing whatsoever. The Prosecution wishes to attach importance to the moment when personnel centres were established. And within that task of theirs, they are disregarding what happened before the personnel centres were established and after the Army of Republika Srpska was established. D242 and P1864, may I remind you. These are documents of the Presidency of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, are decisions of the top state leadership of the then Yugoslavia recognising the rights of these officers, like other members of the JNA. And this happened as far back as May 1992. That is to say, a year and a half before the personnel centres were founded and before General Perisic was appointed Chief of General Staff. And not only that, these two documents set the criteria for their remaining in that army. Members of the JNA who had citizenship of the BH or who wish to remain in the territory of BH are the main criterion for having them stay on and constituting the very core of the officers corps of that army, the Army of Republika Srpska. These criteria were set considerably before General Perisic became Chief of General Staff. On this occasion, I don't want to deal with numbers in detail, Your Honours. We provided part of our analysis in our final brief in paragraphs 3 to 6, all the way up to 330. However, I would like to draw your attention to D113. That is a report of General Zivota Panic, the then Chief of General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, from August 1993, just before Perisic took over the position of Chief of General Staff. On the basis of that report, you will see that the salaries for July 1993 were received by 2.894 officers commissioned and non-commissioned from the VRS, and 1.186 officers from the SVK so the total is 4.080.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I? Is it the Defence position that if a particular activity had been taken place before Mr. Perisic took over the position of Chief of the General Staff, and for argument's sake, that activity is criminal and he comes in and continues with that activity, therefore he is not guilty of that criminal activity simply because the crime had started before he came in? Is that the position?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No. I am referring to other arguments here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Maybe I've jumped the gun. You'll probably come to that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I refer to these figures from these documents, I included those officers from the Army of Yugoslavia who, according to that report, were sent in the meantime to the Army of Republika Srpska because that is the category that the Prosecution included among the persons who are involved in setting up this officers corps of the Army of Republika Srpska. The figures are very specific and exact in that document. The Defence asserts that from the moment when General Perisic was appointed Chief of General Staff until the end of the war, this number of officers who were serving in the Army of Republika Srpska and the Serb Army of the Krajina and were financed by the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia never attained these numbers, these levels, the figures that I just provided. We have provided relevant proof about that as well in our final brief. Now, why does the Defence believe that it is important for you to have these figures? They show the absence of any change in the structure of this officers corps after the personnel centres was established. And that is what the Prosecution has been contending. The establishment of personnel centres did not make an increase in the officers corps possible, and there was no actual increase, nor was the same manpower level maintained, as the Prosecution contends. On the contrary, there was a decline in those figures. That is one of the effects of the personnel centres. Another important position of the OTP, starting from the indictment itself and Mr. Harmon's opening arguments, is that the most important positions in the VRS and the SVK were held by officers who were members of the 30th and 40th Personnel Centres of the Army of Yugoslavia. The Prosecution asserts in their wish to show how significant General Perisic's contribution was to providing those officers, they say that he, General Perisic, provided a group of essential officers, in their words, who were responsible for the crimes in Sarajevo and Srebrenica. That is paragraph 463 and 503 of the final brief of the Prosecutor. The Prosecution exploits this thesis through their famous, I'm going to use that word because they refer to it so many times in court, it is diagram or schedule E. By using it, they want to portray a picture of General Perisic's role in the maintenance and stability of this essential part of the officers corps of the VRS. You heard Witness Skrbic on all of that, page reference 11660 of the transcript. We spoke about that in our final brief. Now, this is our position: All the officers in the key positions in the Army of Republika Srpska, including the officers that the Prosecution defines as being essentially and basically responsible for the commission of crimes, were appointed to these positions considerably before Perisic came to the position of Chief of General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, that is to say, considerably before the personnel centres were established. Now, what are the activities of General Perisic and the personnel centres with regard to their position and the fact that they remained in those positions that they had held already? We haven't heard about that during the trial. You are asked to speculate as to whether they would leave the Army of Republika Srpska, and their positions and duties, had these personnel centres not been established, and had General Perisic not come to the position of Chief of General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia. Let us look at the diagram that I'm talking about. You are going to see that on your screens. That is Schedule E of the final brief of the Prosecution. Mr. Harmon referred to it in his opening remarks. It says what all the names and ranks and positions are within the Army of Republika Srpska, and it says that each and every one of these persons are members of the 30th Personnel Centre. That is the position of the Prosecution. Now let us look at what this organogram looks like within the Army of Republika Srpska at the moment when Perisic became the chief of General Staff, or rather, who came to these positions after the personnel centres were established. Empty. The same mechanism that Mr. Harmon showed you by applying the same method, I'm showing this to you, not a single officer came to the Army of Republika Srpska from among these essential basic officers of the Army of Republika Srpska after Perisic was appointed Chief of General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia and after the personnel centres were established. There were some internal changes in terms of these duties, we know that General Dragomir Milosevic replaced General Galic, but all of the persons we saw a moment ago were already in the VRS before Perisic, General Perisic became Chief of General Staff. It is clear, Your Honours, that the entire structure of the command personnel, the essential personnel of the VRS was within that army. They had the status of members of that army considerably before Perisic became Chief of General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia. Their position in the VRS was defined and occasionally changed in terms of procedure within the framework of the VRS completely independently of the VJ and General Perisic. No matter how hard the Prosecution tried to prove that General Perisic did have a role in their appointments to the positions in the VRS which enabled them or put them in a position of authority enabling the commission of crimes, they failed to prove that. Contrary to that, the Defence put forth a number of exhibits proving that they were appointed to those positions by those responsible in the VRS itself. I invite you to look at paragraphs 272 to 301 of our final brief. Out of the two groups of documents I have just indicated, what it is that you can conclude in terms of the number of personnel, the officer cadre of the VRS, as well as the most important positions of that army, the situation vis-a-vis the time when they were in position of authority enabling the commission of crime did not change. That situation existed far in advance of Mr. Perisic's appointment. Your Honours, the Prosecution did interpret correctly Mr. Perisic's position, however, in his clearly articulated position that those who hailed from Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia and who did not wish to fight for their own homeland and who were VJ officers in his view had no place in the VJ. He said so publicly. It is a legitimate position of a professional soldier and a patriot. However, the evidence we could see during the proceedings speak to his inability to persuade members of the Supreme Defence Council to accept such a firm position which would be binding on him because he was put in that position by his superior, the superior being the President of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and Supreme Defence Council, in these decisions. When his proposal was rejected by the SDC, Perisic lost his position of authority which would enable him to order something to anyone to do anything. He lost his power to issue an order from his position of the superior to send anyone to the VRS. His order, therefore, did not have a binding nature, a binding character. No matter how hard the Prosecution tried to prove that when dealing with his de jure authority. Had those orders been true and real, no other mechanisms would have been necessary that were shown to you by the Prosecution for anyone to be sent to the VRS. That situation also tell us another thing. It shows that when an officer is formally appointed to a position within the30th or 40th Personnel Centre, that could have happened only by virtue of his voluntary departure to the VRS or the SVK. General Perisic speaks to that effect when in paragraph 145 of the Prosecution's final brief they refer to it. If somebody objected to being appointed to such a virtual, I dare say, position in the 30th and 40th Personnel Centre, or in other words sent to the VRS or the SVK, such an order would not have been issued because it was known that if a person did not wish to go, could appeal that decision quite easily. There is not a single proof that anyone complained or appealed their decisions of transfer. However, there is a lot of evidence testifying to the fact that many VJ officers were persuaded to go to the VRS. However, it leads to a conclusion contrary to the conclusion of the OTP on the significant assistance provided by Perisic to their personnel centres in the provision of the officers corps. When the personnel centres were formed, nothing changed in terms of the existing mechanism of persuasion to depart for the VRS and the SVK, in the absence of any coercive measures that could be exercised. Have a look at P317, it is a instruction for co-ordination of the 17th of December, 1993. I won't display it now, I will only provide references. In B/C/S it is page 8, in English page 9. It concerns a period after the formation of the personnel centres and the staffing levels are referred to. It is stated as follows: On the 8th and 10th of December, 1993, a total of seven officers from the VJ responded and an issue of shortage of younger officers personnel is highlighted. Perhaps this may not be the most illustrative example, but let us have a look at something else. Let us look at P1020, which is General Celeketic's report of the 10th of April, 1995. That is to say, 20 days in advance of the events in Zagreb. In B/C/S it is page 4, in English 6. It has to do with the dispatching of officers. It reads: "At the beginning of March, 1995," so a year and a half following the establishment of the personnel centres, "the personnel department of the 40th Personnel Centre invited the commanding officers born in the territory of the former Socialist Republic of Croatia to discuss their volunteer department to the SVK. Out of 600 present officers, 112 stated in a survey that they would be willing to go. In further processing and preparations for the dispatching to the SVK, a final positive answer was provided by 66 officers. On the day of their departure when the time came to board the buses, the officers started hesitating and changing their mind so that only 30 commanding officers went to the SVK (15 officers and 15 NCOs)." General Perisic, at the 37th session of the SDC which is P786 in June 1995, which is over one and a half year following the formation of the personnel centres repeated his proposal he had articulated at early as October 1993 that Mr. Harmon made use of. He asked that those people truly be re-subordinated to the SVK with all the corresponding consequences.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Instead of re-subordinated, it should be transferred.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why such things did not develop exactly as the OTP would wish you have? Well, the SDC rejected his proposal again and reached a firm conclusion, which is something we can see in Exhibit P762. Could we please have it in English. Here it is. In the English version page 5, item J: "The council did not accept the proposal of the Main Staff of the 40th Personnel Centre that officers of the Army of Yugoslavia subject to military service be sent in the future to Republika Srpska, as the service may require. The voluntary principle remains in effect." Therefore, in the summer of 1995 although the personnel centres had been in existence for over one and a half years, they did not produce the effect the Prosecution referred to when putting forth their thesis of significant assistance in the provision of the officers corps. There are two conclusions you can draw from this which are completely contrary to some of the theses of the OTP. The first one the significant contribution in the commission of crime which took place through the provision of the officer cadre, and two, that by provision of the formation of the personnel centres, nothing really changed in the way that cadre was sent. I may add that there is there was no legal mechanism, that is to say, that the orders of transfer could not result in sanctions for anyone refusing to join the VRS. The Prosecution assert that by virtue of the formation of the personnel centres, the position of those officers was institutionalised: those who until that time would serve in the VRS on an ad hoc basis and voluntary basis were, as it is asserted, defined specifically as members of the VJ based on their status regulated within the Army of Yugoslavia. In their view, the view of the Prosecution this amounted in the institutional approach of the transfer of officers to the SVK and the VRS, including those who had already been serving with those armies, as well as those who left subsequently. It is in paragraph 176 of their final brief. The same thesis becomes the crux of their thesis that those officers were then introduced into the chain of command of the Army of Yugoslavia. It is very important for us to ascertain what the matter at hand indeed was, because of Article 7(3) and their thesis that they were part of the officers cadre of the VJ. En route to your final conclusion, the OTP should have established whether they were indeed part of the chain of command of the VJ and whether General Perisic was their superior, whether the relation of superior/subordinate existed. Even if they had been members of the VJ serving outside the VJ, they were no longer part of their chain of command. The army of -- the Law of the Army of Yugoslavia which is Exhibit P197, stipulates that precisely and it was often referred to by the OTP. That law, which provides imperative decisions on the status of those serving outside the VJ, and I will address the specific paragraphs later on, is something that the OTP did not refer to. The Law on the Army of Yugoslavia is quite precise in respect of the status and rights and obligations of those serving outside the VJ. They were definitely outside the chain of command of the Army of Yugoslavia under Article 802 [as interpreted] of the law. They had the same rights and obligations as if they were members of the army unless provided otherwise by the law. So what is essential for our analysis? Please bear with me. I have an intervention for the transcript. It should be Article 8(2) or subparagraph (2).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before you proceed, is it 8 subparagraph (2) or 80 subparagraph (2)? 80 subparagraph (2)?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Article 8, paragraph (2).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Law on the Army of Yugoslavia, Your Honours, has to do with the commanding officers serving outside the VJ regulating their status in relation to their promotion, appointment to duty, transfer, and termination of service, defining that these aspects lay solely with the Ministry of Defence. It was Article 158, referring to Article 152 of the law. The Army of Yugoslavia has no input including the General Staff and its chief. You heard detailed testimony from Mr. Starcevic at page 6969 about that topic, as well as Mr. Nikolic at page 10717. They personally enjoyed the status and had their personal experience based on that. If a VJ officer is serving outside the VJ, all of the aspects of his service were exclusively in the remit of those who were in charge of the armies where they served, not the VJ. That is stipulated by the law. What I said a moment ago when I said, unless stipulated otherwise by the law, we have in this example another binding provision. It has to do with the initiation of disciplinary procedure which should take an important place in your conclusions. The Army of Yugoslavia is competent to initiate disciplinary procedure only vis-a-vis those people who are within the chain of command of the Army of Yugoslavia. In respect of the individuals who are outside of the chain of command of the Army of Yugoslavia, for instance, the law refers to the Ministry of Defence, Article 181 confers the sole responsibility for the initiation of a disciplinary procedure upon the Ministry of Defence. In relation to the exhibits dealing with disciplinary proceedings, we will be discussing those in relation to 7(3). Now, since all the individuals we are interested in right here fall outside of the chain of command of the VJ, the evidence is compelling, Your Honours. In their final brief, the OTP referred to Mr. Starcevic and his analysis of Article 33 of the instructions governing the work of personnel centres, P734. His testimony even gave rise to some questions from the Bench. Those paragraphs -- or rather, let me ask that we call up now Article 33, that same article in respect of which we heard the interpretation of the OTP. Let me just see what page it is. Yes, it's page 7 in English and page 10 in B/C/S. I would like to draw your attention to this article also because I think it's relevant in respect of some other issues. "In keeping with service requirements, professional soldiers and civilian personnel sent or transferred to the KC may be returned, assigned, or transferred" that's what it says" to Yugoslav Army units or institutions with the consent or on the recommendation of the KC Main Staff." In our view, Your Honours, there is no dilemma in interpreting the language of this particular paragraph. In order for someone to return, one has to leave before that, but let's move on. The Prosecution relies on another set of exhibits to prove that the officers of the personnel centres were members of the VJ. These are judgements of the regular courts and military courts where certain officers were asked for some of their entitlements to be recognised. However, these judgements in fact support the position of the Defence that they were outside of the VJ. In fact, that's what all the judgements assert. Yesterday, Mr. Harmon in his submissions referred to Colonel Blagojevic's judgement, which is P1073, I believe. I will not be calling it up now, but look at what the statement of reasons of the military court states, that Blagojevic was outside of the VJ. In no uncertain terms, as a member of the VJ, outside of the VJ ranks. Now, as for this particular judgement and Dragomir Milosevic's case which was before a regular court and not a military court, so the claims made in respect of that must be taken with caution by the Chambers. In those proceedings, no evidence was adduced with regard to the status of those individuals in, for instance, the VRS, as for instance, D330 was never adduced in respect of Mr. Blagojevic. That was the operational map of the Army of Republika Srpska. Or let's look at something else which will overturn the contention by the OTP. Can we now move into private session, please, and look at D120.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session. Do we have confirmation that those screens there are dead? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence argues that the officers defined by the OTP as members of the 30th and 40th Personnel Centres of the VJ General Staff - and I will continue using the term that I consider quite appropriate which is "virtual," so that they were holding virtual positions with the VJ while they were in reality with the VRS or SVK - were not actually members of the Army of Yugoslavia. Besides, it is the OTP themselves who admit that the officers were outside of the VJ at the time. In their final brief, they in fact support our thesis in several paragraphs. For instance, in paragraph 190, the Prosecution states resolutely that General Perisic was able to transfer them back to the units of the VJ. In other words, to go back to where they were not by that point. And I will refer you to some other portions of the OTP brief where the OTP admits that they were not members of the Army of Yugoslavia in a period of time which is important for us. Can we have the break now, Your Honours, because I would like to broach a new topic, albeit a similar one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll take a break and come back at quarter to 11:00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Before the break, I said that the evidence adduced did not demonstrate that these individuals, officers of the VRS and SVK who were, according to the OTP, members of the VJ because of the 30th and 40th Personnel Centres, that they were in fact within the chain of command of the Army of Yugoslavia at the time. Let me continue along the same lines but from a different angle. In order to link these officers up with the VJ, the Prosecution looks to evidence on the formal orders appointing them 0to duties within the personnel centres. According to the Prosecution, if they are appointed to a duty within the personnel centre and the centre is a body attached to the VJ General Staff, then by the same token, they are within the line of -- within the chain of command of the VJ and therefore subordinated, de jure, to Perisic. Even if they were not within the VJ before, as these orders were passed, they would become, in institutional terms, members of the VJ. You will have to assess these positions within the evidence in its entirety. The Prosecution is well aware of the fact that these orders were only formal paperwork enabling these individuals to claim status rights and nothing more. The Prosecution knows that if the matters were as lege artis as they would wish them to appear, in that case there would not have been any need to set up these personnel centres. The Prosecution knows that the top state leadership would in that case not be concerned as to whether the orders would be executed or whether the matter would be taken to court. The Prosecution is aware of all this, because in their submissions they chose to rely on the evidence speaking to these matters. The Prosecution evidence demonstrates that these appointment orders into the personnel centres were not accurate, among other things in their substance in terms of the information that they contained about the actual existence of these units within the VJ as nominally indicated in these documents, and in terms of the actual establishment post which purportedly existed within the VJ and to which these officers were appointed. In paragraph 150 of their brief, the Prosecution refers to Perisic's words as reflected in P709 which is minutes from a meeting, the 14th meeting of the SDC, I believe. And let's have a look at what it is that the Prosecution have to say. Let's look at page 32, if we could have it on our screens, of P709. This is the 14th minutes in 1993, when personnel centres were discussed for the first time, and this is the portion quoted by the OTP in their brief. I will only be quoting one essential sentence. "In order to avoid receiving any complaints from anyone, we invented a temporary formation within the Army of Yugoslavia. We will be appointing them here but in actual fact they are not here, rather, they are in the areas to which they are posted." In other words, Your Honours, a temporary formation is invented, they are not here, rather, they are in the other place where they actually are, which is the VRS or the SVK holding duties which exist in reality and to which they were appointed, pursuant to orders issued by commanding officers of those armies. On the same page, page 33 in English, there is a reference to Perisic's words yet again and Perisic goes on to explain the mechanism envisaged behind this construct. And this is what the OTP quotes: "In the orders we will be, for instance, writing to them: The commander of such and such a unit shall be deployed in a training corps which is supposed to be here, but in fact he is going over there." Hence a unit which is supposedly here is a reference to the Army of Yugoslavia and the units over there, where the individual actually is, is a reference to the VRS. And this is precisely how, when assessing P734, instructions governing the work of personnel centres, which is something that both sides are referring to and specifically paragraph 25 of the instructions that we are referring to in our final brief, you will see that the procedure was defined in detail. As referred in our trial brief. So why is the Defence insisting on the factual, the actual state of matters when speaking about transfers and appointments to duty, and this is something that we discussed in detail in our brief at paragraphs 272 to 295. Your Honours, we are talking about armies here and the functioning of these armies. Appointment to a duty in any army establishes relationships within the service involved and that is a relationship of subordination and superiority. One becomes part of a single chain of command, every member of that army, including the officers that we are dealing with here, gets his or her superior officer. And now this is what matters to me: The orders of that individual have to be obeyed and not observing these orders produces consequences. They have to be held responsible. That is how any army functions and that is how the VRS and the VJ functioned. Therefore, Your Honours, because of these principles, you have to study in detail all the evidence that speaks of such appointments. Both parties have presented such evidence to you, and it is only then on the basis of assessing all of that evidence together, rather than partially, you will come to your conclusions about which army a particular officer actually belonged to when being appointed to a certain duty. In the VRS, these orders on appointment functioned fully, with truthful contents, completely. And if one does not act in accordance with such an order, the mechanism did function within the Army of Republika Srpska. In the orders of the 30th and 40th personnel corps that is not the way appointments took place. I'm going to give you an example now showing what an actual order on appointment is and what a fictitious one is, from the point of view of this situation of superiority and subordination. When the Prosecutor develops his thesis on appointments and the significance of personnel centres, he relies on the so-called group orders on transfers and appointments, so I would like us to deal with a particular case that can be shown through some of their exhibits that they spoke of themselves. Exhibit P2128. It has do with Mr. Tolimir, General Tolimir, because that is what they actually analyse in their final brief. They analyse it in paragraph 175 of their final brief and this is what they say: That is the only order that they invoke. That Tolimir on the 7th of February, 1994, was transferred to the 30th Personnel Centre of the VJ and that this order made formal his service that had started on the 10th of November, 1993. By now I believe that all of us in this courtroom are familiar enough with the fact that the 10th of November, 1993, was the day when personnel centres were established on the basis of an order issued by President Lilic. Before we look at that document, I suggest that we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Slow down, slow down. I heard the interpreter rushing desperately to keep pace with you. Slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please let us deal with this chronologically. So before we look at this document, let us look at something else, but we will be looking at this eventually as well. Let us first look at Defence Exhibit D693. This is a document issued by the president of the Republika Srpska, the date is the 16th of December, 1992. Then Colonel Zdravko Tolimir is being appointed to assistant commander for intelligence and security in the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. You can see that previously he, as it says here, up until now, it says that a bit further down, he was chief of administration for security in the Main Staff from the 10th of June, 1992. Now let us look at another document before we go back to the Prosecution document that I referred to, that is D526. After the end of the war, on the 28th of January, 1997, this is a document of the president of Republika Srpska because it is only decrees, presidential decrees that deal with appointments of generals. General Tolimir is being relieved of his hitherto duties, and you see here which duty he held, the one that we saw a moment ago, from December 1992 onwards; assistant commander for intelligence and security, affairs in the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. Let me digress. Even the Prosecution themselves accept this title of Mr. Tolimir's as a real one, because throughout their brief they accept that Tolimir held this position that we've read out just now, that is paragraph 175, 197, 539, even Annex G of the Prosecution final brief. Now, when we have this picture, let us look at P2128. This order of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, B/C/S page 3 and 4, and English page 3 and 4. A bit further down in B/C/S, Tolimir, that's where it starts, and then it continues on the next page. Now, could I have the next page in English, please. The date of this document is the one that the Prosecution refers to, and that is February 1994. Now, let us see what this document says. It says that on the 7th of February, 1994, he is appointed in the General Staff of the Army Of Yugoslavia as assistant chief in the 30th Personnel Centre in the Main Staff and the date is the one that you recall that Witness Malcic explained to us, I think. 10/11/1993, that is the date. The 10th of November, 1993. A bit further down in the text you see that up until that date, the 10th of November, 1993, he held a position in the 2nd Military District holding the rank of colonel from the 8th of February 1992 in Sarajevo Garrison. Both of these pieces of information are incorrect, Your Honours. You saw a great deal of evidence regarding the structure of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia in all stages of the indictment, before Perisic and after he appointed Chief of General Staff. Remember those organisational diagrams, D195, D196, D197, D198. According to the establishment of the Army of Yugoslavia, there was no Main Staff. There were no corps either, except for the Special Units Corps of the Army of Yugoslavia, that was the only corps that was subordinated directly to the Chief of General Staff. But there are no brigades or corps that are within the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia. You saw the diagrams. There is no such thing. Another piece of information that is incorrect is as follows:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What is meant, now that you are talking about corps in the region, what is meant by the term 1st Army, 2nd Army, within the VJ vocabulary?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would have to be an expert in the field, and I'm not. Armies were the highest military units that covered a certain part of the territory of Yugoslavia, and they had their respective areas of responsibility. These areas of responsibility and these units were outside the General Staff, but the structure -- in terms of the structure, they belonged to the General Staff too. Let me explain this immediately. I think that at the time when General Perisic headed the Army of Yugoslavia, I think there were three armies. Every one of these armies covered a certain territory. In the days of the JNA, I think there were five military districts that later turned into armies, and they covered a certain territory so they were above the corps level in this territorial organisational structure. That's where the army is. The army is superior. I mean, it is a group of corps that cover a certain territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But you just told us there were no corps in that time, so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In the place of the corps there was the army, the 1st Army, the 2nd Army and all these various armies were part of either the JNA or the VJ?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So, in fact, are we to understand that, in substance, the 1st Army is the same thing as a corps but probably bigger?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. Bigger. Exactly. Another piece of information that is incorrect in this document is that Mr. Tolimir was in the 2nd Military District from the 8th of February, 1992 and then as it says here in this document until the 10th of November, 1993. Why? Because the 2nd Military District after the JNA fell apart no longer existed. The 2nd Military District was within the structure of the old JNA, and in that structure -- or he could have been in that structure only until May 1992, so in this period of time that could not have been the case and that is what this document states and that is incorrect. Another example, and I'm not going to explain it any further, but I want to show in these examples how in my view this evidence can be interpreted in the easiest way. As a lawyer I found them very difficult to understand and interpret. P1732, can we please deal with that now. We don't have to put it on our screens, but it's very similar. That is a Prosecution exhibit, by which they wish to show that Vinko Pandurevic was a member of the Army of Yugoslavia from the 10th of November, 1993. It's the same type of order, like the other one. Here it is. Thank you, perhaps it's going to be easier for us to follow if we have it on our screens. The 7th of June, 1994, is the date of this order. It was issued by the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, which we are not contesting, and it says that then Major Vinko Pandurevic in June 1994 is being assigned to, look at this name of the unit, General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, the 30th Personnel Centre, Ground Forces Corps, Light Infantry Brigade. Incorrect, Your Honours. All of us in this courtroom know that. There was no such establishment post in the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia. We saw evidence to that effect. And look at what it says further down, again something incorrect, that up until the moment when this decision was made, he was relieved of duty and sent for training to the General Staff academy already in October 1990. So according to this document, it seems that he is being trained, that he is undergoing schooling from October 1990 until December 1993, and we know that that was not the case. The Prosecution knows that too. There's plenty of evidence to show that. He was in the Army of Republika Srpska. Could we please have D296 on our screens now. The same type of document, appointment, but a different state, Republika Srpska. According to their law of the 8th of October, 1993, the minister of defence is appointing Vinko Pandurevic commander of the 1st Zvornik Light Infantry Brigade in the Drina Corps. That is the actual duty that he held, and that is what Mr. Harmon refers to as well. In the indictment in Schedule E of the indictment in the annex of his final brief in paragraphs of the brief itself, 406, 421, and 438, that was the position he held. That was the actual position he held. We are telling you, Your Honours, that in all these decisions, group orders concerning appointment, the only true information is the one entered there and that pertains to rank and position. And you heard a great deal of evidence about certain status rights that have to do with salaries, benefits that accompany a particular status, and that is the only thing that caused legal effect, but not the way the Prosecution is trying to portray it, that through these orders they enter the chain of command of the Army of Yugoslavia, because other than where it concerns salaries, these orders would have had no other legal effect. But I will come to that later. But even when it comes to salaries, nothing in these orders alters anything that was the situation before that. And you had evidence to that effect. Now, where then can we find this significant contribution of General Perisic to the personnel centres in providing officer cadres for VRS? Now, that these orders did not establish the most important thing in any letter of appointment, and that is the subordination or chain of command, I will show, Your Honour, the chain of command that the Prosecutor is trying to show in their Annex C of the final brief where they say, personnel centres are part of the personnel administration of the Yugoslav Army, and the personnel administration is part of the sector for mobilisation and structural changes of the General Staff of Yugoslavia and that that sector was actually subordinated to General Perisic as the Chief of Staff of the General Staff of the Yugoslav Army. Now, if that was the case, Your Honour, I wonder, and I'd like you to consider this in coming to your conclusions, would this mean that General Mladic was subordinated to Zoric, who was the chief of the personnel administration? Or for instance that he was subordinated to General Matovic, who was the chief of the sector for mobilisation and development of the General Staff of the Yugoslav Army? Is it possible that Mladic was subordinated to them, and this is what the Prosecution's claim is, would it be the case that Mladic would actually abide by anything that this person said to them? And this is the chain of command that the Prosecution is trying to show existed there, and that the Prosecution is trying to claim that it was an attempt to institutionalize the membership of these individuals in the command chain or chain of command of the Yugoslav Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: As I understood Mr. Harmon's argument yesterday, and I think this was also alluded to sometime during the trial, the Prosecution postulates parallel chains of command. I heard Mr. Guy-Smith yesterday contradicting that and saying no, there can only be chain of command. So basing it on the Prosecution's theory, without necessarily accepting it, is it not possible therefore that operationally Mladic wouldn't take commands from the chief of the administration for personnel in the personnel centre, but that administratively that chief dealt with Mladic's salaries, whatever, or -- not salaries, but submitted reports to the paying office of his rank, his position, his service and therefore what he is entitled to as a salary?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will speak about the parallel chain of command a little later, but your question is very to the point, and let me say a few words about it. What you have asked me, and by the very fact that you've put this question, you are actually seeking to find a verbal expression for how their status is regulated through administrative matters and that is indeed the case, but that at the same time, is not the chain of command. The chain of command means issuing and following orders and that is something that Matovic could not do, nor anything else that had to do with any administrative matters. General Matovic could not issue orders to General Mladic. For instance, he could tell Mladic, and this is an administrative matter, "I need a report about the situation with your family, so would you go to your service there and provide that information for me." Now, this is what the Prosecution is claiming that they could issue commands, because they could also issue administrative orders. It is one thing to regulate administratively service-related rights, but there can be only one chain of command, and command and control means only one thing, and in my view this is the red herring that the Prosecutor, Mr. Harmon, is trying to show us here where he is equating these two. We can talk about that, but in fact that is not the case in the case that you have before you. This is just a red herring. It's just conflating two different things. Now, I will come back to that later when I speak of command responsibility and perhaps then you will have more questions that will clarify that matter. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, when you have to draw your conclusions on one of the crucial matters in this case, according to the Defence, which is whether these officers that were mentioned in these group orders, that's how I would refer to them, whether thereby their position in the Yugoslav Army was institutionalised formally, I ask you to ask yourselves the following and the Honourable Judge David put that question at one point, on transcript page 8340 and 8341, to one of the witnesses where he asked the following: "Did the paperwork show one thing and in reality the facts were different?" Perhaps this question was actually directed at something else, but this is very important for our case here. Because the evidence that we have before this Court about the actual reality are actually based on fictitious theses of the Prosecution. Now, the fictitiousness can be seen in another important argument of the Prosecution which relates to command responsibility and effective control. The Prosecution is trying to show that these orders actually indicate that there was effective control and they mention this in their paragraph 782 and 783 in their final brief, however, it is the Defence position that it is in fact these very orders that show that there was no effective control. These orders that the Prosecution in paragraph 783 claims were binding, in reality were not orders to which responsibility would be attached, such as any orders which are not obeyed which relate to military orders. And Witness Starcevic spoke about this on transcript page 5571. And why is this so? Well, because it did not actually correspond to reality. First of all, these individuals were in the VRS and if they disobeyed those orders, there would be no responsibility and no consequences. That's number one. And number two, where the orders were -- where individuals were assigned subsequently, they could only be transferred to those other armies if they agreed to that. Now, this is not something that you will find in any law as a precondition for obeying orders. And why is this so? Because it had to do with transfers that were not regulated under the law, and all of the participants here are aware of that. Had these orders really been binding, there would be no voluntariness and no attempts by anyone to try to talk someone into going anywhere, including by General Perisic. I would now like briefly to digress and mention another argument by the Prosecution that has to do with the assignment to posts. And it is our position that the Prosecution did not show beyond reasonable doubt that Perisic did have the authority to appoint within the VRS itself. And this is what they claim in their final brief, and I believe they also mentioned it in their closing arguments. The evidence shows that all, and I repeat, all appointments to certain positions in the VRS and the SVK were done exclusively within those chains of command without any involvement by anyone from the Yugoslav Army or by General Perisic himself. In order to corroborate their position, the Prosecution in paragraph 183 of their final brief refers to analysis of evidence, P2126 and P1815 in isolation. Those orders that the Prosecution makes a reference to is nothing other than the appointments of these individuals to their posts, or changes in their establishment post. On the other hand, Defence witnesses and Prosecution witnesses as well, Raseta, Orlic, Skrbic, Matic, Novakovic, and I will mention no others, although there are more, testified here that all appointments to duty were done exclusively within the systems of those two armies, the VRS and the SVK. We provided our references in our final briefs in paragraphs 280.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, 280 to 301.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] in other words, both Prosecution witnesses and Defence witnesses tell the same story. Now, in relation to those facts and the witnesses that I just referred to, the Prosecution never in their cross-examination asked any of the Defence witnesses to clarify any of those theses. As for the Prosecution witnesses, Raseta and Orlic, whom we cross-examined, the Prosecution had nothing to ask them in redirect. In other words, they are not really contesting our position, and the Prosecution completely ignores this. It just goes over it. Now, the Prosecution also claims that General Perisic forced officers who refused to go to VRS or SVK to go and if not, that he actually punished them as claimed in paragraph 184 of the Prosecution final brief. In this paragraph, they refer to certain exhibits such as, for instance, P1865, which is an order from the 3rd Army after a meeting with officers from the SVK, where there's a discussion as to who is going to be retired and who is going to be assigned to the personnel centres. Now, this exhibit when shown to Witness Skrbic actually prompted the Honourable Judge Moloto, on transcript page 11895, to ask for clarification as to what the substance truly of that document was. Obviously exhibits such as these cannot prove beyond reasonable doubt that there was coercion on these officers. The Prosecution did not show any witnesses who would speak about these decisions, nor that they would be coerced into retirement if they refused to go to the VRS or the SVK. So there is no evidence, either direct or indirect, that would lead beyond a reasonable doubt to the conclusion that any individual was retired as a direct consequence of their refusal to be assigned to the VRS, as the Prosecution claims. Our colleagues from the Prosecution also referred to the Erak case and Mr. Harmon referred to it by the same name which is mentioned in paragraph 189 of their final brief. The written evidence that the Prosecution is producing here in order to show coercion actually do not prove that there is any coercion. If you look at the notes of a meeting, and this is in document P1896, a meeting -- notes from a meeting between Erak and his commander Zivanovic, where he says -- well, let's wait for the document to come up on the screen. That's P1896. Let us see what these minutes show. These are minutes from an official interview about transfer to the VRS, and we see here that Colonel Erak himself says in these minutes that he refused to sign a letter of appointment whereby he would accept this new assignment, whereby Mr. Erak -- if you look at paragraph A and then the last sentence, the last three lines: "I have refused to be transferred and that is why I did not sign the report," et cetera. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In other words, Colonel Erak states here that he refused to accept this document and that he was entitled to it. We've seen the laws and both laws show that. Any order on transfers is subject to appeals. He refused to sign this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what were the consequences?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He remained where he was, but he did not appeal this decision as he was entitled to. The second exhibit that the Prosecution produced, P1858, also dealing with the Erak case, and we can see in this document the following: We see that Mr. Dragutin Erak did not wait to get the approval of the Main Staff of the VRS in order to return to the VJ, but rather he left the VRS of his own volition. And this was mentioned and something that Witness Skrbic testified to on transcript page 11698. Now, if we look at these two exhibits of the Prosecution together, they do not show coercion. Quite the contrary, they prove voluntariness. They show that there was no authority and no coercion whatsoever that the Prosecution was trying to show General Perisic engaged in. Now, in the last -- in the final brief in paragraph 197, for instance, the Prosecution discussing certain officers of the Yugoslav Army when discussing the case of Kosovo, tries to show that there was an connection between them and the Yugoslav Army, and as Mr. Harmon said, he said that they were going back and forth between the two armies like a ping-pong ball. And in this specific case even in 1999. Now, our claim is that this did not show anything that would be incriminating for General Perisic. They show something else, and we will show that in a moment. Namely, that none of the officers mentioned by the Prosecution in this paragraph and who were on duty in the war in Kosovo in 1999, were on duty in the Army of Yugoslavia during General Perisic's tenure after ending their careers or duties in the VRS. There is not a shred of evidence that that was the case. And for us this is a very important subject that we will come back to when we speak about subordination. A few words about promotions. The Prosecution relied on such documents of promotion and verification of rank to prove both types of liability. Although two days ago you could hear that the Defence when analysed the promotion and verification issues only did so concerning the mode of liability under Article 7(3) in paragraph 426 to 430 in final brief and we would like to invite you to make reference to them. This is where we specifically deal with the thesis proposed about the promotions, verifications and their influence on the stability of the personnel cadre of the VRS and their morale. In our view, the Prosecution asserted that this was precisely their thesis on how the officers were provided. We assert that the conclusion that the Prosecution relied on in order to prove the verification of ranks and its effect on the stability of the army, and that it also is an indicator of effective control is based on an isolated display of certain documents and exhibits. When assessing this issue you will have to decide what it was that the Prosecution managed to prove as a proper indicator of verification concerning the ranks. Whether such rank verifications influenced their stay in the VRS, and whether those rank verifications were a means to exercise authority and effective control by General Perisic over the people who had their ranks verified. The Defence, in its final brief in paragraph 379 to 441 analysed in detail all evidence about rank verifications and its links to the charges against Mr. Perisic. In that regard, we won't repeat ourselves. However, I would like to refer to something we referred to in our final brief as was Mr. Harmon's thesis in his closing argument, and that is the extraordinary promotion of Ratko Mladic. These are P1902, a document issued by President Lilic of the 16th of June, 1994. And P1903, the extraordinary promotion of General Mladic to the same rank in the VRS by virtue of Karadzic's decree. The two promotions did not take place at the same time. He was exceptionally promoted in the VRS 12 days after he had been promoted in the FRY. Mr. Harmon knows well that he holds no evidence of any Perisic's participation in the exceptional promotion of Mr. Mladic in the VJ. He knows that because they read all of the minutes of the SDC in detail as did we. What is important for, you when deciding on the facts, have to bear in mind all the existing evidence which can be correlated to the specific promotion. Because the documents alone say nothing which would enable you to conclude anything about the participation of General Perisic in the exceptional promotion of General Mladic. However, there is an interesting point to note that I would particularly wish to draw your attention to. At all SDC sessions whether exceptional or regular promotions are concerned, there were proposals, and as you could see from the minutes, discussions took place about perhaps I could call them candidates for promotions. utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, what we have been examining in my submissions is related to our submission that you assess and examine the evidence in its totality. You need to cross-reference them and gauge them against each other until you establish facts. I have given you only -- I've referred to only a couple of documents by way of illustration, but of course this is an enormous task before you. If the Prosecution claims that these individuals, by their membership of personnel centres, have had their status institutionalised as being members within the VJ at the time when the conflicts broke out and that by that token Perisic was their superior de jure, then there is only one inference that you can make, only one finding that you can make in that regard, and I will go back to that when discussing effective control because the OTP referred to these orders as proof of effective control. You cannot draw, as the only reasonable inference, not even on the basis of the selection of documents presented by the OTP, and especially not if you regard the evidence in its totality, that they were within the chain of command of the Army of Yugoslavia at the time. We submit that at the time they were solely within the chain of command of their own armies, namely the Army of Republika Srpska and the Army of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina because they were on duties within these armies as the OTP agrees, and as such they were within the superior-subordinate relationships within these armies. As we discussed, the superior-subordinate relationship is established upon appointment to duty. This was the only and true superior- subordinate relationship they were in. None of the individuals we referred to or any of the individuals that the OTP referred to as responsible for the crimes in Sarajevo and Srebrenica were, at any point in time, appointed to any duty or position within the Army of Yugoslavia. In order for them to be able to feature within the chain of command of the VJ, and in order for General Perisic or anyone else for that matter within the VJ to have them as part of the superior-subordinate relationship as envisaged within the Army of Yugoslavia. Your Honour, I do not doubt that in making your findings with regard to the responsibility of Mr. Perisic in respect of aiding and abetting crimes in Sarajevo and Srebrenica, you will always keep in mind the case law of this Tribunal and the way it defines this form of criminal responsibility, as actions directed at assisting and providing moral support to the perpetrators of specific crimes, which constitute substantial contribution to the commission of crimes. Only once you will have established beyond a reasonable doubt all these various elements, will you be able to establish that elements have been satisfied for the actus reus of the accused in respect of the crimes he is charged with, and we claim that the Prosecution has not adduced evidence or provided submissions that would enable you to arrive to that finding with respect to any of the actions by Mr. Perisic relating to their thesis on the provision of the officers corps of VRS in assisting and aiding and abetting crimes in Srebrenica and Sarajevo. I would now like to go to deal with the other form of responsibility, namely that of command responsibility of General Perisic. In a number of legal arguments about command responsibility, both the Prosecution and the Defence referred to the same legal authorities. At the outset, I would like to remind you of what you must be aware of regardless of the submissions we make in our briefs, and which we think is relevant in assessing the evidence and arriving at findings. The theory of command responsibility has been pretty much crystallised through among other things, the jurisprudence of this Tribunal. The case law has provided answers to many issues that have now become part of the standards and part of the international customary law. One of positions that are frequently referred to from the ICTY case law has been formulated in the Celebici appeal judgement at paragraph 303, and I will repeat it although we must all know it by heart now. There the responsibility -- the idea of command responsibility is construed as responsibility of persons who by virtue of the position they occupy have authority over others. But that idea of command responsibility has not been intended to impose liability on persons of equal status. That is the motto, or the guiding idea, that we all follow when dealing with command responsibility. The two main legal issues concerning command responsibility raised by the Prosecution require that we respond to them. At transcript page 14678 and 14679 in relation to what Madam McKenna said, we as a Defence believe that both sides in a superior subordinate relationship need to be aware of the existence of this relationship, whereas the OTP contend that the only parameter of the existence of this relationship is effective control. We continue to hold the position that both parties need to be aware of the existence of a superior-subordinate relationship in order for there to be one. The superior-subordinate relationship is a personal relationship between two individuals and in our view one of these individuals, and that's the subordinate individual, needs to be aware of the existence of the relationship, especially in military structures. The OTP has been building their thesis on the de jure relationships within the army on what is provided by the law. It is inconceivable of the army being operational without the subordinate knowing who his superior is. Of course he doesn't need to know who all of his superiors up the chain of command are, he needs to know who his immediate superior is, or possibly, who the second or third up the level is. Command responsibility as a form of responsibility can be workable within an army only if the individuals involved are aware of the rules of the game. The Prosecution has used the standard of effective control frequently and they want to use it roughshod over all the other elements that may arise and that may be relevant for the determination of effective control. And this is a very dangerous approach, because we know that their effective control exists. Even outside of a superior-subordinate relationship, and we've got many examples from the ICTY case law to testify to that. The superior-subordinate relationship is a relationship between two individuals and the -- and also the insubordination or the duty to obey the superior's orders. And the test of effective control can only be an element that is important for the determination of it.
