utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Concerning this legal matter, it is our position that both participants in the superior-subordinate relationship have to be ware of the existence of that relationship especially within military structures. Let me add another thing, this same Prosecution in earlier cases asserted that there was a presumption of the existence of subordinate-superior relationship in military structures. I believe it was in the Hasanovic or Halilovic case, and it was found insufficient. Another important issue raised by Mr. Harmon, at transcript page 14751 and 14752, in which he asserts that we, the Defence, did not make a distinction between the singleness of command and effective control. They refer to the Popovic judgement, paragraph 2025 and 2026. It is a recent judgement. He relied on that source to corroborate his thesis that a singleness of command does not equal effective control. We, Your Honours, believe that the analysis carried out in the Popovic case that Mr. Harmon relies on is completely inapplicable in our circumstances, because it makes the distinction between effective control and the singleness of command within the same chain of command. It was the relationship between Vinko Pandurevic as brigade commander and Mr. Obrenovic as his Chief of Staff. In that regard, their relationship was analysed trying to see that while he was not in the position of commander, standing in for the Chief of Staff could have exercised effective control, and the Defence relied on the principles of singleness of command. We are in a different case here. The OTP themselves assert the existence of two parallel chains of command, not a single one. In that regard, I wish to draw your attention to the separate opinion of Judge Kwon on this topic, as part of the judgement I referred to. As he puts forth in paragraph 50 of his opinion, because I believe it tallies completely with our interpretation as stipulated in paragraph 73 of our brief. These are two legal matters which will obviously pose a challenge to you in this case. We also wish to draw your attention to the distinction between influence and control. Mr. Guy-Smith addressed it briefly yesterday and Mr. Harmon did not mention it at all. This Defence team is deeply convinced that this case is the best example of the difference that needs to be drawn between influence and control. This is the case which can openly and crystal clear show to us the extent of influence when it exists, when it does not, when it is exercised without reaching the threshold of control. Based on all evidence presented, you cannot establish beyond a reasonable doubt that there was effective control that crossed that threshold. By virtue of that, you cannot conclude that there was the relationship of superior/subordinate between Mr. Perisic and those designated by the Prosecution as crime perpetrators. When analysing the relationship between influence and control, please bear in mind that in this case we move within the boundaries of a clear set of the way the game is played. There was a single chain of command and we know how it worked. Before I move on to the issue of influence itself, I wanted to mention another important thing and this is where we differ from the Prosecution. However they did not mention it in their final argument, but they did in their final brief. We have opposing Tribunal jurisprudence in that respect. We assert, as we put forth in paragraph 80 of our final brief, we support the jurisprudence confirmed in several cases including their appeal phase before this Tribunal which states that the liability of the commander can exist only if there was effective control over the perpetrators at the time crimes were committed. We are aware of the existence of two appeals with different positions and this is ours. Only at the time of the crimes there must be effective control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Can you cite all those, all three of them, please. Sorry, the stenographer didn't hear me, I was saying can you cite us all three judgements. The one that you go with and the two that go against you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think I mentioned three. There were several. However, there are two on appeal that are contradictory and I will refer to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. There were two.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Please bear with me. Halilovic. Just a second. The judgement in the Halilovic case, paragraph -- first, the trial judgement because I have a few references. Perhaps not to complicate things, I can tell you that it is all in our paragraph 80, footnote 130 of our final brief. Perhaps that is the simple way to go about it. These are the references we invoke to support our arguments, the opposing position was taken in the Oric case and the appeals judgement, and I believe the OTP relied on that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Footnote numbers 131.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to move on to the relationship I wanted to discuss at some length, that is to say the existence of influence and control within the parallel chains of command. The OTP in this case, regarding command responsibility, had to face the jurisprudence encountering a significant obstacle, namely, how to charge Perisic without compromising their own thesis of the responsibility of certain people in the chains of command of the VRS and the SVK. They had the dilemma of how to establish a thesis on the responsibility of Commander Perisic when they already had existing indictments against Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Martic and the Prosecution to assert that Mr. Perisic was not their subordinate. It is not in question. Their impossible mission, they formulated in the indictment by forwarding a thesis that Perisic delegated the so-called operational control to Mladic and Celeketic, as well as Novakovic, in paragraph 6 and 35 of the indictment, and that his command responsibility was, as they say, parallel to Karadzic's, which is what they said in their opening statement, and at transcript page 379 and 380, as well as in their final brief. In the final brief, they articulate the concept in paragraph 804 where they say that there was this unique situation in which we found ourselves in this case. In the army, commanding is the gist of -- the prerequisite of the functioning of the system. There's an order which needs to be obeyed. You asked about that, Your Honour, and this is how I understand the thesis of the parallel chain of command. There is no army in the world which is based on a parallel chain of command. The Prosecution know that, and then they created the concept of the so-called administrative control, trying to compare this still unique case to an existing model. Expert Melvin did not help the Prosecution in that regard. There's absolutely no correlation that could compare NATO or the allied concepts with our case. I say our case because we are all familiar with it. In this case, an officer left an orderly structured military system, entering, fully and completely, another organised system. He is assigned his position in the other system, his only and single superior who promotes him, who commands him in any respect. He also enters a completely regulated system of military discipline and military judiciary and we know it functioned. The Prosecution assert so as well because they state that Karadzic could have initiated disciplinary procedures against his subordinates in the VRS. In the final brief, it seems to us that the Prosecution gave up on the assertion put forth in the indictment, that is to say, that Perisic delegated operational control to the commanders of those armies, because there's simply no evidence to that extent. There isn't a single shred of evidence to show that he delegated such control to Mladic, Mrksic, Celeketic and Novakovic as asserted by the Prosecution in the indictment. We discussed it in detail in our brief in several paragraphs, and I will tell you what they are, it is 148, 154, 858, 985 and 995. Let me add something else, in a single chain of command, there could be several superiors exercising direct or indirect effective control and they can bear the responsibility, but not outside the chain. Armies are structured and function in a way so as to obey one superior. If that does not work, the army does not work. What it looks like in real life rather than in an isolated lab can be seen if we are look at the Zagreb charges. Could we please move into private session for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Defence assert, as we have explained in our brief, and in the first part of our closing argument that all officers of the VRS and the SVK, designated by the Prosecution as direct perpetrators and members of the VJ, at the time the crimes were committed were not within the chain of command of the VJ. No matter how hard they try to show that their status in the personnel centres tallies with the command chain of the VJ, they themselves have to admit that while they were on service in the VRS and SVK, they were not within the VJ chain of command. If they are outside the VJ, then at the time when the crimes were committed, Perisic was not their superior. If there is no relationship of hierarchy, then there is no superior-subordinate relationship and we all know that that is one of the three essential elements of command responsibility. Now I'm going to move on to some of direct evidence that shows about absence of control on Perisic's part over his alleged subordinates. Please assess all the evidence in its totality. I would like to deal with something now that Mr. Guy-Smith mentioned yesterday and that was the policy of the state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Chamber can assure you the Chamber will look at the entire evidence. The Chamber can assure you that the Chamber will look at the entire evidence. We have been reminded of this several times during the Defence argument and we just want to make that assurance to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your support. I think that I speak for all the participants in the proceedings. I have this concern, I think we all have this concern that we are trying to look at all of this together at a given point in time. I would like to point this out to you, when assessing something that is called context. I spoke about that in my opening statement when you look at a document, and you are probably going to say now that that is certainly what you are going to do, but it is important for us to say that documents always need to be looked at within context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like to say something about this context of state policy as an important factor for assessing responsibility and facts. Although expert Melvin could not assist the Court very much in explaining the general principles of command and control, in his methodology he mentions in paragraph 2.1 -- could I please have that on the screen. P2772, page 4 in English, page 4 in B/C/S, he speaks of context, and he says that context is very important, as we have said, to assess the functioning of any chain of command. And that there are many non-military factors that affect that and he ends with a particular position that I would like to quote. And this is what he says: "Actually, command at highest level, strategic level, can never be isolated from governmental policy and direction. Thus, the exercise of command must always be viewed in the appropriate context, if motivation were to be understood, reasons, and desired and actual outcomes of the commander's decision." I think that you heard the interpretation, so you don't have to look at the rest in English on your screen, because we would need to move on to the next page in English in that case. In this case, we have evidence related to command and control at the highest strategic level that is most directly linked to policy as such, political decisions and top state leadership. Although the Prosecution wishes to stop the positions of the state leadership of the FRY and their policy in the early stages of the war as something that was defined and unchanged, that was actually not the case. The evidence that they produced before you shows that at least from April 1993 and especially from the summer of 1994, there was a permanent and genuine wish of the state leadership of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to stop the war and the leaderships of Republika Srpska and the Republic of the Serb Krajina as well as their military leaderships should accept the peace settlements offered by the international community. Namely, the Contact Group Plan, as well as plan Z-4 pertaining to RSK, all the way up to the Dayton Accords. There's a great deal of evidence that points to this and we dealt with part of it in our final brief. However, Your Honours, now we have the opportunity of referring to some of that evidence in open court. Evidence that shows unequivocally on the one hand the objective of the state leadership of the FRY to have the war ended, and on the other hand, this very important decision -- distinction between influence and what the Prosecution wishes to portray as control. I know that you are going to assess all of that evidence within the context of the time-frame involved. Let us first look at P778. In B/C/S, it is page 26, and in English, it is page 39. Very briefly. It is the 30th session, or rather, sorry, the 25th session of the Supreme Defence Council in August 1994, after the Contact Group Plan was rejected. I'm providing the context. And that was after the FRY imposed sanctions against Republika Srpska. President Milosevic is speaking about the relationship between the two political and military leaderships. Very briefly, the first paragraph: "Yes. Therefore, the war option is absolutely pointless. From a moral point of view, I don't think that we should be beating ourselves in the chest as to who is amongst us a better Serb, or a Serb by profession. We have had that over the past few years, but now you can find such people by the dozen." Now page 41 and 42, again it is Milosevic who is the speaker. The end of the page, this is what Milosevic says: "All of that is being put at a risk by a fixation that 'perhaps one or 200ths of the territory could be acquired if the plan is rejected.' In my view," says Milosevic, "this is not worth prolonging the agony of war, of sanctions against Yugoslavia and all other difficulties that could be place on the shoulders of the Serbian people." Finally, page 44, again it is Milosevic. It is page 29 in English. This is his conclusion: "Therefore, the answer to this question is, we must apply all possible forms of pressure towards having the peace plan accepted. It is out of the question that any reasonable person could opt for a continuation of war and the drawing of Yugoslavia into the war conflict. This was the major and most important danger, the drawing of Yugoslavia into the armed conflict, which we managed to escape." Milosevic said all of that at that session. P779 is what I'd like to call up now. This is the 28th session of the Supreme Defence Council. The 2nd of November, 1994 is the date. In English it is page 32, and in B/C/S it is 30. This is what Milosevic says: "It is not the question anymore whether they can accomplish that goal." He is talking about the Army of Republika Srpska and the leadership of Republika Srpska. May I remind you of the context. November 1994, we, I beg your pardon, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia imposed sanctions on Republika Srpska. This is what Milosevic says: "We told them on time that it was impossible to achieve the goal that they wanted to achieve and that politics is the art of the possible and not the art of the impossible. It is simply impossible for the international community to go along with the fact that two-thirds of the population, including Croats and Muslims, are crammed into less than half of the territory." Then Perisic, General Perisic, page 34 in English, the very same transcript. Page 32 in B/C/S. The context is the attempts to influence the leadership of Republika Srpska to accept and support the plan of the Contact Group. Now, in that context, General Perisic says: "I suggest that we try to persuade them if we still can do anything," the reference is to the leadership of Republika Srpska, "otherwise they will face a complete disaster. It is not only that they will face it, but such a situation will have dramatic consequences for the Serbian and Montenegrin peoples." Now, look at another short dialogue from that session. In English it is page 36, and in B/C/S, 34. This is what General Perisic says: "It would be good if any factor could get involved that has any influence on them in order to try to bring them to reason." And then Milosevic says: "Momo, the army is the sole factor that has influence on them and you know very well that you cannot do anything there." When you read this entire document, you will see what this refers to and who, but it is clear that it is the Army of Republika Srpska, then Perisic says: "Mr. President, at least we can invite them and we can try to persuade those people before this audience. There are multiple reasons why I'm asking you to do it." Milosevic says, "Call Mladic. I think we can talk again." And then, Your Honours, this is P734, or rather, 743, I'm not going to ask to have it displayed. Sorry, P743. Those are the conclusions from that session and I suggest that when you analyse the evidence, you look at conclusion number 4, where an unequivocal decision is being made on the basis of this dialogue, and it says: "Caution the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska and try to bring General Mladic in for a talk." That is the end of that conclusion. Please look at P794 for a moment, the 31st session. Let us look at the context, the 18th of January, 1995. We have heard a great deal of evidence about that, the officers of the VRS no longer received their salaries, sanctions were imposed, and there is a lot of discussion at that session about how the leadership of Republika Srpska can be persuaded to accept the plan of the Contact Group. Let us see what President Milosevic says. Page 50 in English, and B/C/S is 45. It's just a short sentence. The second paragraph, Your Honours, these are Milosevic's words: "However, on the other hand, the army should not be a prisoner of a crazy policy there led by that leadership. That is something that Perisic tried to explain to them on several occasions, as we all did, but unfortunately, it was unsuccessful." Can we now adjourn for the day three minutes early because I will be discussing the same topic, but I'd have to call up a different document, so perhaps this would be a good time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Lukic. We'll then adjourn for the day and come back tomorrow at 9.00. Same court. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
